All parties, however await the issue of the Dresden Conference. From Household Yvor s. WORK! AN ANECDOTE. A Cavalry Officer of large fortune, w ho had distinguished himself in several actions, having been quartered for a Jong time in a foreign city, gradually fell into a life of extreme and incessant dissipation. He soon found himself so indisposed to any active military service, that even the ordinary routine became irksome and unbearable. He accordingly solicited and obtained leave of absence from bis regiment for six months. But, instead of immediately engaging in some occupation of mind and body as a curative process for his morbid condition, lie hastened to London, and gave himself up entirely to greater luxuries than ever, and plunged into every kind of sensuality. T ie consequence was a distrust of life and all its healthy offices. He became unable to read half a page of a book, or to vv lie t lie shortest note : mounting his horse was too much trouble ; to lounge down the street was a hateful effort. His appetite failed, or every thing disagreed with him ; and lie lie could seldom sleep. Existence became an intolerable burden ; he therefore determined on suicide. With this intention lie loaded his pistols, and, influenced by early associations, dressed himself in his regimental frock-coat and crimson sash, and entered St. þÿJames sPark a little before sunrise. He felt as if lie was mounting guard for the last time ; listened to each sound, and looked with miserable afl'ection across the misty green toward the

llorsc Guards, faintly seen in the distance. A few minutes after the officer bad entered the park, there passed through the same gate a poor mechanic, who leisurely followed in the same direction. lie was a gaunt, half-famished looking man, and walked with a sad air, Ins eyes bent thoughtfully on the ground,

<0 © a % AT 2 SL and his large bony hands dangling at his sid þÿ S. The officer, absorbed in the act lie meditated, walked on without being aware of the presence of another person. Arriving about the middle of a wide open space, he suddenly stopped, and drawing forth both pistols, exclaimed, Oil, most unfortunate and most þÿ wretched man that I am ! Wealth, station, honor, prospects, are of no avail ! Existence lms become a heavy torment to me! 1 have not strength þÿ I have not courage to endure or face it a moment longer þÿ! I With these words he cocked the pis- < i s , and was raising both of them to His lie ;d, when Ii is arms were seized from behind, and the pistols twisted out of His fingers. He reeled round, and lieheld the gaunt scarecrow of a man who had followed him. þÿ What are þÿyou? stammered the officer, with a painful air ; þÿ llow dare you to step between me and death þÿ? þÿ 1 ain a poor, hungry mechanic answered the man, þÿ one who works from fourteen to sixteen hours a day, and yet finds it hard to earn a living. þÿ My wife is dead þÿ my daughter was tempted away from me þÿ and I am a lone man. As I have nobody to live for, and have become quite tired of my life, I came out this morning, intending to drown myself. But as the fresh air of the park came over my face, the sickness of life gave way to shame at my own want of strength and courage, and I determined to walk onward and live my allotted time. But what are you ? Have you not encountered cannon-halls and death in all shapes, and now want the

strength and courage to meet the curse of idleness þÿV The officer was moving off with some confused words, but the mechanic took him by the arm, and threatening to hand him over to the police if he resisted, led him droopinglv away. j This mechanic's work was that of a turner, and lie lived in a dark cellar, where he toiled at liis lathe From morning to night. Hearing that the olficcr had amused himself with a little turnery in liis youth, the poor artisan proposed to take him down into liis work-shop. þÿ The officer olfered him money; and was anxious to escape ; hut the mechanic refused it, and persisted. 11c accordingly took the morbid gentleman down into his dark cellar, and set him to work at His lathe. The officer began very languidly, and soon rose to depart. Whereupon, the mechanic forced him down again on the hard bench, and swore that if he did not do an þÿhour w s ork for him, in return for saving liis life lie would instantly consign him a policeman, and denounce to him for attempting to commit suicide. At this threat the officer was so confounded, that he at once consented to | do the work. I When the hour was over, the mechanic insisted on a second hour, in conse- J quence of the slowness of the work þÿ it 1 had not been a fair þÿhour l s abor, in

vain the officer protested, was angry, and exhausted þÿ had the heartburn þÿ pains in liis hack and limbs þÿ and declared it would kill him. The mechanic, was inexorable. þÿ If it does kill þÿyou, said he, þÿ then you will only he where you would have been if 1 had not stopped þÿyou. So tiie officer was compelled to continue his work with an inflamed face, and the perspiration pouring down over liis cheeks and chin. At last he could proceed no longer, come what would of it, and sank hack in the arms of his persecuting preserver. The mechanic now placed before him Ins own breakfast, composed of a twopenny loaf of brown bread, and a pint of small beer; the whole of which the oik eer disposed of in no time, and then sent out for more. Before the hoy who was dispatched on this errand returned, a little conversation had ensued : and as the officer rose to go, he smiling placed liis purse, with lus card, in the hands of the mechanic. The poor, ragged man received them with all the composure of a physician and with a sort of dry, grim humor which appeared peculiar to him. and the only relief of liis otherwise rough and rigid character, made sombre hv the constant shadows and troubles of life. But the moment he read the name on the card, all the hard lines in his deeplymarked face underwent a sudden contortion. Thrusting back the purse and card into the þÿofficer s hand, he seized him with a fierce grip by one arm þÿ hurried him, wondering, up the dark broken stairs, along the narrow passage þÿ then

pushed him out of the door ! þÿ ou are the fine gentleman who tempted my daughter away þÿ! said he. þÿ l þÿ your daughter þÿ! exclaimed the officer. Yes, my daughter: Ellen Brent þÿwood! said the mechanic. þÿ \rc they so many þÿmen s daughters in the list, that you forget her þÿname? þÿ I implore þÿyou, said the officer, þÿ to take t liis purse. þÿT rtiy, take this purse! If you will not accept it for yourself, I entreat you to send it to her þÿ! þÿ Go and lmy a lathe with þÿit, said the mechanic. þÿ Work, man ! and repent of your past life þÿ! So saying, he closed the door in the þÿofficer s face, and descended the stairs to liis daily labor.

To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis ! Sir, I noticed in your paper ot the 2d instant, the names of the gentlemen, who were elected as members of the Burgher Council, and who, I presume, will enter on their new functions on Monday next. These Representatives, collectively, will be able to accomplish a vast amount of good, if they perform their duties conscientiously, and in a straight-forward manner, only keeping before their eyes, the welfare of the community at large. Such a course as tiiis, if adopted by them, must necessarily tend in an essential manner to forward our future progress, and crown their efforts with success. We have been favored with line weather þÿ the planters are all alive to their own interests þÿ so that in reality, with proper laws and regulations steadily administered, St. Croix lias little, we hope, to (car. It is true we have some heavy burdens to hear þÿ the heaviest is our unmerciful Tariff, which is as heavy as a millstone, and so high as to deprive us of the advantages of American trade. If those duties were reduced to a lower scale, we would hail it as a boon of immense benefit to the poor. They arc the great sufferers by the Tariff; for while many of the luxuries of life are taxed with a very trilling duty, the heavy impost is made to fall on the very articles which constitute the poor man's staff of life. To this may lie added, that the wages of mechanics and other labourers are very low at present, þÿ so that a working man after paying house-rent and other expenses attendant on the support of a wife and

family, has really very little left in hand at ihe end of the week. With many (to use a familiar expression) it is merely from hand to mouth ; and consequently any measures that will tend to meliorate the condition of this class of people, will be quite a God-send. Wishing our new Burgher Council every success in their deliberations for J the common good, 1 remain, Tour obedient servant, A NATIVE. < lm.>tiaii<1ed, 9th January 1851.

M. GUIZOT ON EDUCATION. M. Guizot lias written a long letter to a provincial paper, the Experana, of Naney, detailing at great length his disapprobation of the recently-adopted measures with respect to public instruction. The French Institute, by recent regulations, was requested to elect three of its members to represent that body in the Council of Public Instruction. The Institute naturally turned their eves tow- i y ards M. Guizot, than whom no one was so competent to form a just appreciation ol such matters. M. Guizot refused to be put up as a candidate, and M. Thiers was elected in his place. In this letter M. Guizot assigns his reasons for refusing to represent the Institute in the council of public Instruction. In the course of his observations he says þÿ I he education ot the rising generation is a field naturally open to all labors, and there is in that field an arbiter naturally called to choose between the persons engaged. Philosophers may have maintained that children belong to the State, and that it has a right to seize on them at its pleasuse ; Governments, in the violence of religious persecutions, may have carried away children from their parents to have them educated in the faith of the national church. Hut such doctrines and such acts shock the moral and supreme instinct of the human rare. Children are placed by the law of God under the authority of their parents and it is in the family circle that the natural right of education resides. Attempt to contest that right directly and in prin-

ciple ; declare that the parents shall not be permitted to bring up their children themselves, and that they must hand them over to public establishments, laic or religious; you will sec with what energy universal feeling and common --ensc "will repel such a tyranny. F.sibiishmcnts of education, distinct from tnc family circle, exist only to supply its place and to do what it cannot or will not do itself. There are two great substitutes, two great natural auxiliaries of the family circle, the Church and 1 he State. The Church because as religions instruction belongs to it by right, it is naturally (it to give at the same time f lie moral education which belongs so intimately to religions instruction. þÿ The State, because, as it represents society in ils totality, it is charged to provide for all the interests, moral or physical, which claim its action. In modern -oeicties, where the government is essentially laic, and where civil life and religious life are essentially indistinct, the presence and action of the State in ilie field of public instruction are not

fluty. The free competition of the Slate and of the Church in public education, and the free choice of families between the establishment of the two, is the idea to which natural facts, considered in themselves, and independently of every system more or less exclusive or factitious, evidently conduct. Particular and temporary circumstances,

A ©31 © I A T 2 3. the slate of men's minds, anterior regimes, the necessity of precautions and of transitions, can modify or retard the application of that idea ; hut it is not the less the true and simple idea, and, I may even say, the right, prevailing in this matter; and when its application is possible, it ought to be applied, I am convinced that the clay of this application has arrived, or will speedily arrive for our country. The principle which serves as the base for the new law, as for all the laws passed, or proposed on this subject for the last forty years, may lie put in practice in many a manner ; the government of public instruction may be shared between the State and the Church on very different conditions and in very unequal degrees; hut by none of these combinations will be obtained either the peace which is sought for between these two powers, or the moral empire with which both one and the other must he invested in order to suffice for llu ir admission. Of what use would be peace itself between the clergy and the university, if, in order 1o obtain it, the two bodies were placed in a situation such as that their action should he enervated, their authority extenuated, their dignity compromised 1 We have need of infinitely more than the peaceful understanding ol the powers called on to struggle against the moral evil of which our society is a prey, and which threatens to seize on the rising generation even more than on the retiring one. þÿ We have need of the most energetic

efforts, the most persevering ardour; and Ihese efforts, that ardour, that desire ot success it is not combinations þÿ loaded with negotiations and trammels that can give them to us þÿ but the regime ol real liberty and of strong competition amongst 1 lie masters of youth. Let the clergy and the university freely display all their moral resources; let them come to an understanding, and advance with emulation in the field of national education þÿ they will still have great difficulty in working it with success and in its totality. Is it necessary for mo to sa\ that 1 by no means desire to deprive t lie State of the right of general superintendence, which belongs to it over everything that comes within its range ? þÿ That right may he perfectly well exercised in a manner not to cause any injury to real liberty and to the mutual independence of the different establishments of public instruction, laic and religious. You perceive that I have gone far away from the new law. As a measure of transition, it may prove useful þÿ it may even he necessary ; but it does not appear to me good either as a system of organisation, or as a means of only a matter of right hut a matter of true and durable compromise ; it will not attain, I conceive, either the general object of education, or the special end of pacification for which it is intended 1 should consequently he hut little calculated to aid in its execution. The more I consider all that is passing around us, the more every false position is hate-
ful to me. Nothing is more like a false position than to lend a hand to a work

on the merit and success of which one does not believe. It is a great blessing, however dearly it may he purchased, to lie able to remain, not only by one's act ions, but also in appearance, in the truth of what one thinks and desires, I do not feel disposed to quit such a position."

THE MOTHER'S FIRST !>f I would wish every mother to pay attention to the (tifl'ernce between a course of action, adopted in compliance with the authority , and between a conduct pursued fur the sake of another. The first proceeds from reasoning : the second flows from affection. The first may be abandoned, when the immediate cause may have ceased to exist ; the latter will he permanent, as it did not depend upon circumstances, or accidental considerations, but is founded in a moral and constant principle. In the ease row before us, if the infant does not disappoint the hope of the mother, it wiil he a proof, first of affection, secondly, of confidence. Of affection--for the earliest, and the most innocent wish to please, is that ot the infant to please the mother. If it he questioned, whether that wish can at all exist in one so little advanced in development, I would again, as I do upon almost all occasions, appeal to iho ex perienee of mothers. It is a proof, also, of confidence. þÿ W henever an infant has been negleetcd; when llic necessary attention has not been paid to its wants; and when, instead of the smile of kindness, it has been treated with the frown of severity: it will he difficult to restore it to that quiet and amiable disposition, in which it will wait for the gratification of its desires without impatience, and enjoy it w ithout greediness. If affection and confidence have once gained ground in the heart, it will be 1bc first duly of the mother to do every
tiling in her power to encourage, to strengthen, and to elevate ibis principle - -I'extn/iz it.

PHYSICAL EDUCATION. The revival of gymnastics is, in my opinion, the most important step that has been done in that direction. Tingreat merit of the gymnastic art is not the facility with which certain exercises are performed, or the qualification which they may give for certain exertions that require much energy and dexterity; though an attainment of that sort is by no means to he despised. Hut the greatest advantage resulting from a practice of those exercises, is the natural progress which is observed in the arrangement of them, beginning with those which, while they are easy in themselves, yet lead as a preparatory practice to others which are more complicated and more difficult. There is not, perhaps, any art in which it may he so clearly shown, that energies which appeared to he wanting, are to he pro duced, as it were, or at least arc to be developed, by no other means than prac

lice alone. This might afford a more useful iiint to all lliose who arc engaged in teaching any object of instruction, and who meet with difficulties in bringing their pupils to that proficiency which they had expected. Let them recommence on a new plan, in which the exercises shall be differently arranged, and the subjects brought forward in a manner that will admit of the natural progress from the easier to the more difficult. When talent is wanting altogether, T know that it cannot be imparted by any system of education, lint I have been taught by experience to consider the eases, in which talents of any kind are absolutely wanting, but very lew. And in most eases, I have had the satisfaction to find, that a faculty which bad been quite given over, instead of being developed, bad been obstructed rather in its agency by a variety of exercises which tended to perplex or to deter from further exertion. And here I would attend to a prejudice, which is common enough, concerning the use of gymnastics ; it is frequently said, that they may be very good for tbose who are strong enough ; but that those who are suffering from weakness of constitution would be altogether unequal to, and even endangered bv, a practice of gymnastics. Kow 1 will venture to say, that this i sis merely upon a misunderstanding of the first principles of gymnastics: the exercises not only vary in proportion to llie strength of individuals ; but exercises may be, and have been devised,

for those also who were decidedly stillering. \ ml I have consulted the authority of the first physicians, who dedared, that in eases which had come under their personal observation, individuals aflected with pulmonary complaints, if these had not already proceeded too far, had been materially relieved and benefitted by a constant practice of the few and simple exercises, which the system in such eases proposes. \nd for ibis \ery reason, that exercises may be devised for every age, and for every degree of bodily strength, however reduced. I consider it to he c-seutiab that mothers should make themselves acquainted with the principles of gymnastics, in order that, among the elemental v and preparatory exercises. they may be able to select those w hich, according to circumstances, will be most likely to suit and benefit their children. If the physical advantage of gymnas lies is great and incontrovertible, I would contend, that the moral advantage resulting from them is as valuable. I would again appeal to your own observation. You have seen a number of schools in Germany and Switzerland, of which gymnastics formed a leading fea ture : and I recollect that in our conversations on the subject, you made the remark, which exactly agrees with my own experience, that gymnastics, well conducted, essentially contribute to render children not only cheerful anil healthy, which, for moral education, are two

On one time a young officer scoiled at the idea that it required so much time to preach a sermon as ministers pretended, and offered a bet that he would preach half an hour on any passage in the Old Testament, without preparation. Mr. Morrison took the bet, and gave him tor (he text. ' And the ass opened his mouth and he spake.' The parson won the wager, the officer being rather disinclined to employ his eloquence upon that text. On another occasion Morrison entreated an officer to pardon a poor soldier for some offence he had committed. The officer agreed to do so, it he would in return grant him the tirst favour lie would ask. Mr. Morrison agreed to this. In a day or two the officer wished that the ceremony of baptism should be performed on a young puppy- The clergyman agreed to it, and a party ot many gentlemen assembled to witness the novel baptism. Mr. Morrison desired the officer to hold the dog, as was customary in the baptism of children and said, As am a minister of the Church ot Scotland, I must proceed according to the ceremonies of the Church.' ' Certainly,' said the officer, ' I expect all the ceremony.' ' Well then, major, I begin with the usual question. From the St. Thomas Times, Jan. 11. The short passage of the American Barque Gov. Oxiioem, Captain Davis, which arrived here yesterday morning, furnishes us with dates from New York to the 30th. After carefully examining our files we find very little which could be pronounced of much interest. Business in Washington, both political and private was suspended there, as usual at Christmas. The Stores and Markets and public offices were closed and both Houses of Congress had taken a recess. Many of the Members had gone home to for the Washington Monument, bearing spend the recess with their families. Although Congress would meet the day after Christmas it was not intended to do any business of importance till after New A var's. The political calm prevailing in the country was noticed the other day by Mr. Clay as favorable to the consideration of the tariff subject. Mr. Clay however, did not assert that the calm was real and would continue, but he expressed a hope it would. General Scott is, judging from the city papers and their Washington correspondence to be the man likely to be run for at the next Presidential election, but who will be the opposing candidate no mention is made. M'd le. Jenny Bind had arrived at < harleston. The steamer which conveyed her there, is said to have experienced very severe weather, and reports it one time had been circulated of her being lost. The political news of the island is not of much importance. The quietness had not been disturbed since our last advices, and no fears were entertained of a new invasion. Four Spanish frigates of war the Guia de Vigo, Esmeralda, Europa, and Primera dc Gustemala þÿ from Cadiz, with about 1,300 officers and soldiers, entered the port on the 9th of December, and t he troops disembarked on the following day, in presence of the Governor General. COLONIAL POLICY. Copenhagen, December, 1850 In a late discussion in the House of Representatives (Folkething) on the interpellation of the Honorable Alember, Professor Krieger, on the nature and extent of the power of issuing or sanctioning provisional laws in the Colonies, granted the superior government, the Minister of Finance, Count Sponneck, expressed himself as follows in regard to the future Colonial policy, The Minister of Finance : þÿ I shall with the greatest pleasure comply with the wishes of the honorable interlocutor about furnishing this house with all the elucidations he lias asked for, in order to comprehend this matter ; 1 have ordered all the papers to be prepared and they will immediately be laid on the table of the house. It will be seen from them, not only what orders have been issued provisionally, but also bow far they have been sanctioned here, finally which of them have not been sanctioned and on what grounds. 1 believe that sonic exaggerated opinions have been formed on the use which has been made of the powers to issue provisional ordinances by the Governinent-Commissaay sent out in 1848, which powers were considerably limited in 1849. It is however certain, that the said powers have been used, and that some points of great moment have been touched; it is likewise certain, that with the exception of the law, regulating the trade, and navigation of the island of St. Croix, which was sanctioned by both bouses here, no other law has received such positive

sanction. The case has been this, that amongst the ordinances, sent here for sanction, some have not been so fully developed by motives, that this Government have thought themselves fully justified to lay them before His Majesty, for his signature, and against others the Government have had serious objections, and it will be seen from the order sent out in 1849, that it was not only thought desirable to limit the extraordinary powers granted the Government-Commissa-

ry, but aho to bring about a nearer connection with the laws hitherto existing, anil a greater harmony with the Danish laws and the actual circumstances of the colonies, than it appeared to be the case with some of the proposed laws. Much time is lost in sending and returning documents, and this is particularly the cause why the law regulating the Police Courts has not been either finally sanctioned or recalled. In regard to that law, I have corresponded with the .Minister of Justice, and returned it to be examined a-ncw, and the Counsellor for the law-department of the Government, who was at that time here, was ordered to assist the Governor in framing it a-new, allot' which will fully appear on examining the papers, which I shall produce. Some of the orders or laws in question have however received a preliminary sanction, because it v, as thought that the Government-Commissary had a right to expect to be made acquainted with Ilis Majesty's views on the measures, generally taken by him. although not considered fully ripe for a definite sanction. This is for instance the case in regard to the Regulations for the work of the free labourers, of which three different editions exist, one for St. Croix,- another for St Thomas and lastly one for the island of St. Johns. With regard to these regulations the government of the Mother Country had many doubts ; but as it is generally necessary to be very careful in making modifications m this country, regarding the colo-

nics for want of local knowledge, so it was evidently still more the case here, as the welfare of the colonics depended materially on the success or propriety of this measure. And as it has been >tatcd from many sides, that these regulations were proper, and having been proved to be. so, by procuring order and peace, and from the fact, that the system is working better in our islands, than in any other colony, where the emancipation has been carried out, it appeared to the Government, that sufficient grounds existed, if not for llis Majesty's sanctioning the same in ail its detail, at least for expressing in a Rescript of 1849, that Government approved of the general measures taken by the Commissary for maintaining order in the colony. At the same time lie was ordered to make such proposals for modifications of the regulations, as experience might after some time prove neecss irv, anil only alter having received these reports the time may he considered to have arrived for obtaining llis M ijcsty's (inal sanction. In us far as regards other colonial niath and circumstances, (he Government have been somewhat in doubt. The fundamental law contains not/ting expressly about the colonics. During the discussions of the constituent assembly it was made a question, whether a Law for the Colonics would be one of the measures immediately to be proposed by Government. The proposals made at the time uerodropped not that they were considered unnecessary, but because " the Colonial I. aw"
w .is required io be given at a time, w hen

T ATI it was not possible for the Government to do so. I am likewise in a position not to be able to propose " the Colonial Law." 1 have not yet been able to obtain a proposal from the Government-Commissary for the final organisations of the relations of the Colonies, and 1 do not doubt that vou will agree, that it is impossible to propose such a law, before at least a good part of the necessary prelimary materials have been received from the Government-Commissary. It is also a question, whether such a law can be drawn up here, or if it should not more properly be made in the Colony. Li that law, it must, amongst other things, be clearly stated, what is to be the relation of the legislative powers, in as far as regards the Colonies, to the Houses here. Until this is fixed by law, the Government have been ot opinion, that the ruies hitherto prevailing should be followed, by which the " States" were not called to deliberate on what did not directly influence the affairs of the Mother Country. The Government have taken the opinion of the Attorney General, and the result has been, that such measures, for instance, the law about the navigation and trade ot St. Croix, from its very nature, required the sanction of the "Rigsdag;" but that laws, relating merely to the internal affairs ot the Colonies, should not he sanctioned in this way, as long as the " Colonial Law" is not given. The Government do therefore intend, until otherwise decided, to lay such laws and proposals, which ought to come before this House,

for its sanction, on the tabic of the House, to be discussed and sanctioned here, and the others will merely he approved of by resolution in the name ot His Majesty. Such Royal resolutions have also hitherto been the means by which the laws of the mother country, /. i., the Law of Heirships, of 18 15, were extended to the Colonics. I do not deny that much is left in suspense and uncertainty, and I see no other means to make an end thereof, than by a Colonial law. No one feels the want of that law more than myself, for the Minister, who is connected with the Colonies, is, in as far as regards administrative measures, often in t he greatest difficulty, Irom the circumstance, that nothing is left for the linal decision of the Colonics themselves, and that every matter is to be reported home, whereas this Government at home has not the local knowledge required to decide all these special cases. 1 have taken the necessary measures for the preparatory steps required, and " 1 hope to lie able to lay a draught of a Colonial Law" before the next Rigsdag " it is however not quite certain. For the rest, 1 beg the lion, members to suspend their judgment on the measures taken by the Government-Commissary, until they have examined the papers 1 am © <oin< © to lav J on the table of the House.
Mr. Paine s great discovery, for generating light and heat from water at an expense comparatively nothing, and in illimitable quantities, is about to be tested in New York. The conditions of

the bargain are, that Mr. Paine shall with one of his machines produce at a nominal expense þÿ say five cents per thousand cubic feet þÿ gas enough to light the Asterhousc for six successive nights. Before he commences, the parties interested, ate to deposit one hundred thousand dollars to be paid over, as soon as the test is declared successful. This, is bj way of a bonus or guarantee, in case there should be a failure, to pay over to him the sum of one million, which is to render those parties part proprietors of the invention. Tinadvantages derivable from this important discovery, are incalculable, and it will now be tested on a scale so extensive, as to remove, if successful, all doubt as to its vast utility. Light and heat, and motive power, will be producible at all times, and without any sensible cost, out of materials which abound every where without price. Steam will be superseded, or rendered so cheap as to bo of common use in the most ordinary de partments of labour. There will be no more use for fuel þÿ coal mines will be left unworked þÿ trees no longer cut for fuel. Every thing which requires light or heat, will become cheaper, and though there may he heavy individual losses in the sudden disturbance of the value of machinery and capital, in the end every ont will he better off. These are wonderful changes indeed yet there are many of great science and ability who affirm, that Mr. Paine's invention is all that it assumes to be. The result of this interesting trial, will be

Hamburg, January 18. Tiif. Journals of this place and Berlin, have put forward divers speculations, for the most part erroneous, not only as regards the person and sentiments, hut the nature of the mission with which Count Sponneck, Danish Minister of Finance, is intrusted. A few words explanatory of the objects ol this mission þÿ words resting upon good authority may not therefore he totally þÿ irrelevant. The mission with which the

intrusted to the Court of Vienna, and subsequently to that of Berlin, has for its object, not to decide, but to pave the road for arriving at an understanding with Germany relative to the final settlement of the question of the Duchies, as regards their relations to Denmark and to each other. Through an interchange of opinions relative to the respective and views of all parties interested, Count Sponneck will, it is hoped, he enabled to form a judgment as to the most practical and attainable terms of arrangement, ar.d through that judgment Denmark be guided in making its intended proposals to Germany. The apprehension entertained by divers German journals that the Danish Finance Minisier is the hearer of proposals at variance with the pretensions and interests of Germany, is unfounded. The printed rumours of dissensions in the Danish Cabinet regarding the .Schleswig-Holþÿ stein question þÿ the circumstance that Baron Pechlin, designated at first for the Dresden mission, having declined that mission ; and a totally erroneous estimation of Count þÿSponneck charac- s ter and political principles þÿ have combined to give rise to these errors and apprehensions. There never has been, nor ever will he, dissensions in the Danish Cabinet, or among the Danish representatives and people, as to the broad principles on which a settlement of the Schleswig- Holstein question is to he based ; that is to say, as to the maintenance of the political rights and relations of Denmark over and with Schleswig, and the
paramount necessity of closing the door upon all further encroachments of Germany, by drawing a political line of demarcation between Denmark and the Confederation, so distinct as to preclude

all further cavelling or doubts ns to where the rights of Germany terminate, and where those of Denmark commence. Opinions have certainly varied in I tenmark as to details of settlement, as to the terms necessary for carrying out this principle, and as to the concessions that might be made without endangering it. It is possible that a difference on these points has prevented Baron Pechlin from devoting his valuable services and the fruits of his oft-tried experience to this mission. At the same time the choice of Sponncck may be regarded as most judicious, and is far from indicating any unbending or unreasonable disposition on the part of the Danish Cabinet. The Danish minister of Finance, although the youngest, is one of the most distinguished members of the Cabinet. The admirable manner in which he has conducted his department under the most trying circumstances, lias obtained for him a high character with the Danish Chamber and people, and fulfilled the expectations of those who urged lus nomination to the post he holds. With the revenues of the country reduced more than a third by the defalcation of the Duchies þÿ with enormous calls upon the treasury for the support of a war, w iged during nearly three years, not only against the insurrection, but against all Germany þÿ with the burdens of the national debt, and civil list falling exclusively upon Denmark þÿI ropcr, Count Sponncck lias contrived not only to raise the nece.'Sary funds for meeting the many

engagements of the country, but has maintained the credit of Denmark in tact, whilst large deficits, and something worse, stared half the assailant Govcrnmenls in the lace. Count Sponncck has not only risen high in the estimation of his countrymen as a financier, but as a practical, patriotic, and independent statesman. He is the representative of no political idiosyncrasy or party, but endeavours to suit his views and conduct to the force of those circumstances wherein he expects to derive the greatest sum of practical benefit for the country. The opinion that the Count will arinc at during the course of lus mission will, therefore, obtain the confidence of his colleagues and countrymen, as being the unbiased judgment of a dear-sighted and essentially practical man. It is for this reason that his selection must be regarded as of good augury. The following, unless we have been utterly misinformed, may be regarded as the outline of the polic y intended to be pursued by tbe Danish Government in regard to the Schleswig-Holstein question, and which M. de Sp- nneck will probably develop as occasion may require. The negociations of peace, which terminated on the so-called pair pure et sim- />/. of the 2nd July, 1H50, entered into on t He basis of the preliminaries of peace concluded under British mediation oil the 10th July, IS49 þÿ that basis, it will be remembered, indicated a political separation of the duchies ol Schleswig and

<8 'di 8 1 it þÿA OS, Holstein, and a union of Schleswig and Denmark, under a certain degree of provincial independence. The parties not being able to come to an accord upon the terms of this arrangement, the peace of July last was concluded under a mutual reservation of all rights and pretensions. This treaty brought peace to Germany, hut not to Denmark. A sanguinary and deplorable war was illumined by the act of signature þÿ this war has been protracted during six months between Denmark, and t lie insurrection backed by the moral and more than the moral aid of Germany, the Governments of which were unwilling or unable to execute the engagements and obligations they had contracted. The proposals made by Denmark on the basis ot the separation of the duchies and provincial independence þÿ nothing more, ol Schieswig þÿ proposals approved by Great Britain, but opposed by Prussia þÿ wi.l no doubt from the groundwork ot the present Danish propositions. Denmark, it is well known, declined to make ulterior concessions at a time of heavy pressure, and siie was at that period encouraged in her resistance by Ragland and by Russia. JVollung has occurred to induce her to modify her resolutions, nor h.is any tiling taken place that can justly induce the Great Powers to urge or recommend her to do so. To Prussia and Austria she is under no oL ligations. They have simply performed an original duty, alter a most detrimental delay of six months, which delay has caused Denmark the lives and limbs uf

nearly S,0U0 of her devuted and loyal sons þÿ devastated the fertile districts of South Schleswig þÿ occasioned the wanton annihilation of a flourishing town, the destruction of villages and farms, and augmented the heavy burdens itillieted on the Danish people bv the prolongation of an unjust and unnatural war.

Any other basis than that of a separation of the two duchies would not only be the triumph of Germany but of the insurrection, and the utter ruin of Denmark. It would keep open the wounds which have already nearly bled to extinction ; and it would expose her to a recurrence of similar calamities at any moment when Germany might he exposed to internal convulsions. It is impossible that .Schleswig can he a particle suspended as it were between Germany and Denmark, a fief of Denmark, of Holstein, and of Germany at one and the same time. That would be a political incongruity, insupportable at least to Denmark. Her provincial independence may be ceded as a guarantee for the rights of her mixed nationality and peculiar position, but in all essential respects she must be regarded by Denmark as a political integrality of the kingdom þÿ that is, if Denmark does not think fit to admit that all her efforts and sacrifices for the last three y ears have been exerted in vain. Sueli appears to be the most probable basis on which þÿSponncck s mission is to be conducted, the only basis that is con-

sistent with the vital interests of Denmark þÿ the only basis that would receive the undivided approbation of the Danish nation, from the King down to the humblest peasants who have rallied round their þÿcountry s standards prepared to sacrifice life and goods in their defence. The Holstein troops have commenced their retrograde movement in the direction of Rendsluirg. Kiel and Altona. þÿ The Austrian troops are passing the Kibe with as much expedition as circumstances permit, by the ferry boat at Artlenburg. The whole will have crossed over before the 27th.

From the St. Thomas Times, Feb. 22. A visit to St. Croix. We find in the " Barbados Agricultural Reporter," of the 8th February (in a letter addressed to the Editor), a few remarks from the justly esteemed, scientific Planter, Dr. P. Lovell Phillips, of Barbados, who lately visited these Islands, and delivered an excellent practical lecture " on Agriculture'' to the Agricultural Society of St. Croix, which has lately been published by Mr. ilatchett, of that Island; and as it is highly desirable that we should benefit as much as possible by the criticisms of men apparently wiser than ourselves, we give the following extract of his letter, as far as relates to our Sister Colony : þÿ " We proceeded to Santa Cruce (as the writer not improperly spells it), by a small sloop from St. Ivitts, which we chartered for $50, and which furnished us with a very tolerably comfortable mode of transit, although I confess it, scarcely agreeable, even running down with a fair wind of the strength we had it. We left St. Ivitts at 10 a. m., and reached the East end of Santa Cruce the next morning about 8, having been obliged to lie oil' for an hour or two for a pilot, the entrance to the harbour being exceedingly intricate and dangerous, though well buoyed-oft'and delightfully sheltered within, being the only instance that I remember of a town and harbour directly to windward of one of our Islands. The town of Bassin we found to be built with great regularity, and with wide streets, clean and airy, and possessing, besides a very respectable block of Government buildings, a

number of private dwellings which spoke of prosperity, tho' rather in the past than the present þÿtime; some few buildin". indeed, indicated a tendency to revival, which 1 trust may largely be realised and augmented throughout the affairs of this beautiful and fertile little Island. I am bound, however, freely to confess that the Hotel at Bassin presents not the smallest possible indication of anything but the most precipitous downward course. All happiness and prosperity to the landlord, but may it be in some other line of life ! Poor man! I could not but pity him, over-burthened as he seemed to be with a ruinous old house, in size far beyond the requirements of bis business, and a head evi dently little fitted for enabling ir any one else to take " ease himself in his Inn 1" All this is perhaps not purely affricultural © ; nevertheless I take it that he "Crown" docs in some degree shew the retrograde character of the late movements in Santa Cruce, þÿ at any rate i is in keeping with them, for unfortu nately the Colony has undoubtedly been going the wrong way for some time past. I trust, however, and believe, that this retrograde movement has come to an end, and that the Island of Santa Cruce may take that position amongst the sugar producing countries, to which she s s o well entitled by her natural capa-

££_ <8 IB <D I AT 1 3« bilities, and by the intelligence of her Planters, than whom I certainly never met with any set of men more desirous of improvement. " The sudden, and in some measure ill-timed emancipation of the negroes, no doubt acted most injuriously upon the interests of the Island, and threw it back immediately in every respect ; but I am happy to say, that so far as my observation and enquiries went, I had every reason to think that society has been re-arranged upon a new basis, in a most satisfactory manner, by the truly exemplary code of regulations promulgated by Governor Hansen, with the assistance of most excellent advisers. To many, no doultl, these regulations would appear stringent as regards the labourer, but they are no less stringent as regards the employer. If the former is bound under contract to work by the year for the Estate on which lie is domesticated, the latter is bound not only to furnish the labourer with a home, which is beyond all comparison the best labourers' home I have seen in any part of the world, but to pay him in money and in provisions exceedingly liberally, even though he should not have absolute occasion for his services during every working day in the year. 1 say every working day, for Saturdays as well as Sundays are exempt from the contract. So well does this system work, that even although there are in Santa Cruce, as elsewhere, mischief makers, who endeavour to render the people discontented, complaints are seldom preferred by either labourers or employers before

the magistrate, and when complaints are made both parties seem to admit the justness of the sentences, even when unfavourable to themselves. 1 trust that nothing may ever disturb the good feeling which thus scents to exist between the two classes in Santa Cruce, and then I conceive that all will find that a real benefit has been conferred by emancipation, especially if the Danish Government eventually grant to the Proprietors the compensation to which they seem fully entitled. However this may he, 1 feel great confidence in the spirit of improvement displayed by the Planters, when brought to bear in earnest and in faith upon the great capabilities of their Estates þÿ capabilities which 1 must say are at present very far from being fully developed. In the sugar making department the Planter of Santa Cruce has long stood unrivalled, so far at least as quality and price are concerned; a question may possibly be raised whether ever in this respect the Santa Crucians derived as much profit from a given amount of canejuice as some others who do not make as fine a sugar; but in Agriculture there can be no doubt that he is very far behind hand, and, fortunately for him, he is not insensible to this. Of the capabilities of the land I entertain a very high opinion ; much of it is of a deep tenacious black character, and if properly tilled would, I have no doubt, make large returns þÿ far heavier than at present ; whilst other portions of the Island are of a hillv character, with a

much lighter soil, on a subsoil, of marly matter, and in some districts the lime formation prevails. The system of cultivation is scarcely varied in these dif- ferent districts, at any rate not more so than the physical character of the sur- r face formation renders imperative ; and I must say that this uniformity is so far unfortunate, as it extends to the greatest extent a radically had " In Santa Cruce, as system. with lis, the Planter has many difficulties to contend with, but that which is paramount to all others is, the want of rain þÿ I might almost say of daily rain ; but even such a blessing would fail of doing all the good which it might, if counteracted and rendered in a great degree n u gator) by the formation of high banks in the first place, and the preservation of these in as unbroken a state as possible. By such means the lighter rains are retained on the suilace to be rapidly evaporated, and the heavier are forced to run ollj carrying with them the best part of the soil and manure. The consequence of all tins is that the canes are tor the most part stunted, and, I believe, are never fully developed, whilst, whatever growth they attain, they are more woody than juicy. 1 he pains and skill bestowed upon the formation of these high and narrow hanks is something truly marvellous, and more creditable to the industry of the country than to its agricultural principles. The labour bestowed on these hanks must absorb a large portion of that which is at command, and leaves

no room to wonder at the frightfully grassy condition of the fields in all sta ges ol the crop. Again, all the mischiefs that are visible or can be conceived arr perpetuated and augmented by the ex reedingly close planting universally pursued in Santa Ciuce. We have so lately moved out of our glass houses, that we have littlr right, and i trust, less inclina I Kin, to throw stones at our neighbours' windows; but really it is lamentable to see the pains and cost bestowed upon a method of planting, the only and certain effect ot_ which must be to prevent tlx canes from being l'ully developed. I think the banks from the centre of out hole to that ol the next, cannot be more, than three feet ; and of distances between the canes there are none, for the plants are set in rows nearly as thick as they can be, þÿ at any rate they are not further apart than the length of two plants ! VV ell, the result is what might have been expected, þÿ hard banks, high banks, weeds, and close planting do their work effectually, and the return front the best lands seldom exceeds two hogsheads, whilst I rather think most estates would gladly compound for one hogshead per acre fur all the canes cut. It must, however, be understood that more than half ol the year's crop consists of ratoon canes up to the fourth and fifth years (and on to the tenth and fifteenth in some rare cuses.) Half a hogshead per acre is a very fair return for much of this ratoon lund, and a good deal I apprc hend, would not give more than a quar-
ter to an acre. I should observe that of course tliis sugar is very strong, and

being skilfully mixed with that from the plant canes, contributes to the beauty of the sugar, for which this Island is famed. Still I cannot but think that even if a shade of excellence were lost in the equality of the sugar, it would be compensated by the enormous increase in quantity which might he extracted from the land, which seems to me to yield to none in fertility and capabilities. This is moreover proved by the return obtained from at least one Estate near town, which is amply manured and highly cultivated, and which is said to make in enormous return, say 2£ hogsheads per acre round, including ratoons. This is a famous example, and I am happy to think that there is every prospect of this beautiful Island increasing rapidly in its productions, for I never saw a community more anxious for improvement, and already ploughs and other implements are coming largely into use, whilst increasing attention is being paid to the subject of manures. " In the manufacturing department, little seems to be left to be desired, þÿ a beautiful, coloury, and grainy sugar being produced by a remarkably simple but efficacious arrangement ; in some instances clariliers worked by separate tires are used, and three iron tayches, þÿ in others there are live tayches, and then the fourth and filth are used as clarifying vessels. Such are the old batteries; the improved apparatus consists of three iron tayches and three clarifiers, worked by the waste steam from the engine driving the cane mill þÿ the boiler of that

engine being in turn worked by the waste lire from under the tayches þÿ the whole being so skilfully arranged as to enable every Estate to abound in mcgass. The liquor is brought to the cracking point in the clarifiers. the steam shut off, and the scum removed carefully, the steam is again let on, and fresh scum removed. In the tayches there is no skimming except in the third, any little lirt on the others being brushed back o the preceding vessel. The skips are very large, three I think to a hogshead ; two of them are sent successively into the same cooler, then into another, and when the first is returned to the crust is broken up, and, floating on the fresh syrup, is carefully removed. The coolers are deep, and the sugar being boiled rather low and in considerable mass, does not granulate thoroughly for two or three or more days, and a little syrup generally remains on the surface to the end. It is really a treat to see the sugar in the hogsheads. I shall not attempt to describe particularly the beautiful apparatus on Captain Christmas' Estates, because in fact it partakes more of lie character of refinery work than of a mere muscovado factory; the syrup is passed through immense charcoal filters, boiled in vacuo, potted, syruped, cured, crushed and packed in hogsheads, and sent home to compete with refinery goods, and carries with it my best þÿ wishes, as competing in fact with crushed sugar made from slave produce. It is, however, almost exclusively sent to

3 "J\ ©& 6 ATJ3, Copenhagen, where the government encourage the import of sugar from its colonies, and moreover it is virtually excluded from the British markets by a differential duty, carefully adapted to sheltering the British Refiner from the effects of free-trade. " Apologising for the very imperfect character of these hasty notes, and earnestly recommending all whom it may concern to go and see for themselves, I remain, your obt. sevt., 1'. L. P. January 12th, 1851.

H0LSTE1N. Our Hamburg correspondence of the I Ith inst., gives some further details of the occupation of the citadel of ltendshurg by the Danes. After the llolstein troops had quitted the fortress on the 8th the works were occupied by the Austrian troops, and it was generally believed that neither the citadel nor any ot the forts would be given up to the Danes. But at 11 a.m. on the 9th it was stated that the Danish troops were marching upon the fortress, and at 12 o'clock the Danish commander sent a trumpeter with a message to the Austrian general, who, surrounded by his staff, immediately proceeded to the gates of the fortress, when he met the advanced guard of the Danes. The Austrian sentinels in the citadel were next relieved by a Danish guard. The llolstein populace were silent witnesses of this spectacle, and the only demonstration consisted in a few boys singing the Ilolstein " Mecrum-schlungen." It is stated that with the citadel, the Danes obtained possession of 4ft cwt. of gunpowder, which were deposited in its vaults. It is likewise stated that the fortifications of llendsburg will be demolished and the first proposal in this respect has emanated from Russia. þÿ Evening Mail, Feb. 14

A cabinet-maker of that place, a habitual drunkard, having been condemned to six months' imprisonment for ill-treatment of his wife, determined to put an end to bis existence. þÿ « OCA-1 þÿ LADIES' ARITHMETIC. 11 v a confirmed bachelor. Ladies have quite a different system of calculation to what men have. Look at the peculiar way in which tliev calculate a«res. Why! they are quite an age behind the present generation þÿ at least, the generation of men for a man is, þÿ figuratively said, as he grows older, to approach into his second childhood, hut a woman does so literally, inasmuch as she becomes every year one year younger þÿ a rejuvenating process by which, if she lived long cnoughhe would ultimately reach the happy period when she was carried about in long clothes, and took a tenacious delight, peculiar to babies, in pulling gentlemen's whiskers. In fact, I wonder that, carrying out this retrograde movement, a married lady, as she advances in years, does not re-appear on the stage of life as the hall-room girl, and throw off the matronly title of Mils., to put on the more flowery salutation of Miss. It would he more consistent with the representation of figures þÿ we mean, arithmetical figures þÿ though it might be a little at variance with the appearance of personal ones. My belief is that the female mind has no correct sense of numbers. It belabors and rolls out figures as cooks do paste, making them as thick or as tliin as it pleases to fit the object required. I have noticed a largeness of liberality of measurement in most of their calculations, which redounds greatly, in this calculating age, to the generosity of the sex. It is quite opposite to the self-

measurement which they apply to themselves. Whereas the latter is distinguished by a narrowness of result which almost makes us suspect that Subtraction has been largely at work ; the former is crowned with a roundness of figure which leads us strongly to accuse the sum total of having been gained by the corrupt agency of addition. In fact, my suspicions arc so violent on this head, that 1 always adopt the following plan when I am at a loss to know : How to correctly ascertain the age or a lady. I first ask the I.ady accused her own age. 1 then inquire ot her "dearest friends." I next ascerdifference 1>\ five years to forty), and, dividing that eouuts (which frequently varies from tain the difference between the two nc- þÿ . I add iliat quotient to

a the lady's own representation, and tlie result is the lady's age, as near as a lady's age can he ascertained. Example: Mrs. Wellington Seymour, gives herself out to he 28. Her friends, Mrs. M'Cabe, Mrs. Alfred Stevens, Madame Cornichon, and Miss Jerkins, indignantly declare that they will eat their respective heads off it she is a day younger than 46. Now the disputed account stands thus : Years
Mrs. Seymour's age, as represented by her friends, 46 Mrs. Seymour's age, as represented by herself 28

Difference between thetwo Accounts 18 That difference has to be divided by 2, which, I believe, will give 0. It that is added to Mrs. Sey mour'sown statement, the result obtained will be the answer required. Accordingly Mrs. "Wellington Seymour's age is 37 þÿ a fact, which, upon consulting the lamily Bible, I find to be perfectly correct and I only hope þÿ Mrs. S. will, some day, forgive me for publishing it. There are many other eccentricities in female arithmetic, such as increasing twofold the amount ot a gentleman's fortune, and diminishing fiftyfold the amount of a lady's and a þÿ general proncness, besides, to magnify figures, O 7 leading them, at times, into , t range errors ot cx«iggeration» which would debar them from following the works of numerical fidelity, like M'Cul- profession of a penny a-lincr, or «' writing loch's Commercial Dictionary." Hut as I do not love the female mind particularly for its eccentricities, but rather for its beauties, I shall close the door upon this ungallant subject ; for, it a woman is good and beautiful, it matters but little how old she is.

She was a poor little girl indeed, then ; she was lonely and neglected, and would have been very unhappy, deprived of the kindness and care so necessary to a child, if it had not been for a peculiar gift. The little girl had a fine voice, and in her loneliness, in trouble or in sorrow, she consoled herself by singing. In fact she sang to all she did ; at her work, at her play, running or resting, she always sang. The woman who had her in care went out to work during the day. and used to lock in the little girl, who had nothing to enliven her solitude hut the company of a cat. The little girl played with her cat and sang. Once she sat by t he open window and stroked her cat and sang, when a lady passed by. She heard the voice and looked up and saw the little singer. She asked the child several questions, went away, and came back several days later, followed by an old music master, whose name was Crelius. j ness she sang with a hurst of outflowing lie tried the little girl's musical ear and voice, and was astonished, lie took her to the director of the ltoyal Opera of 1 Stockholm, then a Count 1'ulie, whose truly generous and kind heart was concealed by rough speech and a morbid temper. "Well," exclaimed he at last, " if you will not take her, poor as I am I will take her myself, and have her educated for the scene ; such an other ear as she lias for music is not to be found in the world !" From the New York Morning Express, February 10. Extraordinary lloiililc tinnier. Boston, Feb. 8. In the woods at Braintrcc, yesterday, two hunters discovered the dead bodies of two persons frozen stiff, þÿ they laid side by side. One of them proved to be a woman in male attire. It appears that they reached Quincy, near Bruintree, in November last. They stated that they came from Ohio and passed as half brothers. After a stay of 8 days, during which the man worked at boot making they went into the woods and committed suicide. The female was about 17, | and educated, and of higher station than the man. We find in the Boston Transcript the following additional particulars concern- j ing the dead bodies found in the woods near Ouincy, Mass, referred to in the above despatch : þÿ On an inspection of the bodies, they were identified as those of a man and woman, both entire strangers in the j rism, Ac. place, who suddenly disappeared on the 2(ith of November last from the house of Mrs. Mark Wood, in Quincy, where they had boarded for a very few days inder the name of Green, and stating hat they recently came from Cincinnati. From all appearances on the spot, 'o rether. with some recollected circumstances, it was evident that both parties had committed voluntary suicide by shooting. The man held a common horse-pistol in hand, having apparently hot himself in the mouth, while the woman was shot in the side, in the region of the heart. Both were very respectably dressed, in male attire þÿ the man wearing a brown dress-coat, dark

pants and vest, and black hat ; and the woman, plain pants, brown sack coat, dark vest, and cloth cap. Previous to disappearing, the man had worked some ten days at boot-making, for Mr. Whitcher. of (|uincy ; but after reading in a Boston paper on the morning of November 2fith, an account of a runaway couple, he left his work, and proposed to his companion that, as they had not been out much in the vicinity, tie wished to take a walk. They left together, which was the last seen or tieard of them, until found as described. The same morning, the woman was heard to remark, that though she was young, she had seen trouble enough for O a life of fifty years. The deportment of both had been unexceptionable, but there was some indication of hidden sorrows, and their history was kept entirely secret, which m ide them objects of considerable curiosity. The age of the man was apparently about 28. and that of flic female, who was quite handsome, about 18. þÿ Both were well educated, and had evidently been once far differently and more favorably circumstanced.
The i a i i: Tragedy in Quincy. þÿ Nothing has jet been ascertained, to throw additional light upon the recent

« AT1 tragedy, which has caused so much ex- i citement in Quincy and the immediate vicinity. Upon a thorough examination of the articles in the room occupied by the two deceased persons, at the house of Mrs. Wood, the following sentence was found written on a piece of paper ; in a book in the room : " To the oppressed and down trodden ; to those who are bowed even to the grave with grief- þÿ to the suffering and alliicted, I would say þÿ Fear not, but follow Truth ; tread boldly where it leads, and with philosophic calm, and a majestic bearing, go on, through the j seemingly mysterious process of death ; Truth still guides with light revealing to the a wakening and more interior senses, a habitation of harmony and blessedness."
Besides this, two or three sheets of letter paper, were found, closely written in pencil, evidently by a person of superior education. They contained speculations relative to spiritualism, mesme-

One fact, which possibly may lead to some information in regard to the deceased is, that upon the right arm of the man, between the wrist and elbow joints, is marked, in indelible ink, an oblong wreath, and also a likeness of some female, the latter of which, he had been repeatedly heard to say, he wished was obliterated. þÿ Ibid, Feb. 12.

To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis! Sir ! As it would be of immense benefit to our community, that a Savings' Bank be established here, to afford an opportunity to those persons, who would avail themselves of the advantages of such an institution, I beg to throw out my humhie suggestion on the subject, trusting, that some more competent person, will follow up the hint and see it carried into execution. It is an undoubted fact that, in countries where Savings' Bank, have been instituted, the inhabitants are encourged to practice economy to a greater extent, than in those places where no such institujtions exist. Look for example, at our sister þÿcolony St. Thomas ! the last statement of the Savings' Bank there, up to 15th March, exhibits the balance of deposits as high as $25,278 4(5 cts. which augurs well for the promotion of the object of this bank. Such an establishment amongst us would be of incalculable benefit to the inhabitants both of the towns and country. In the first place, the towns people would be urged on to a stricter practice of economy þÿ many of them would lie able, from t heir weekly savings, to realise a sum, which, in case of sickness, would tend to alleviate their wants, and when infirmity and old age creep on, they would be less dependant on others to assist them. As far as the country people are concerned, the advantages, to these, would even he still greater. Never, perhaps, were thefts so common in the country as at the present day ; and the reason is: that the

people have no secure place wherein to deposit their money ; they entrust it to each other, and the consequence is that a facility is thus offered to thieves, to help themselves at their neighbours' expense. Whereas, if a Savings' Bank were established here, it would be very easy for the people, say of a Saturday evening to enter their deposits, whatever the amount might be, receive their acknowledgement, and go home perfectly assured that their earnings were in the right place, and out of the way of danger. There would be no difficulty, 1 should think, in instituting such a Bank þÿ it is within our reach þÿ there are many gentlemen in this town, who would undertake the management gratuitously, as is done in St. Thomas, and I would consider the man or men, that would take a leading part in so desirable a work as public benefactors fo the Island. 1 remain, Sir, Your obed't. servant, A NATIVE. Since the departure ofthe last steamer for Panama the Indian difficulties have been on the increase rather than otherwise, and murders, robberies, and reports of hostilities, collisions and battles have been rife. Efforts have been made in the Legislature to raise funds and State troops for carrying on the war. þÿ One of the þÿGovernor a s ids, J. Neely Johnson, Esq., has been despatched by his Excellency to the scene of disturbances, to act on the part of the State with the U. S. Indian Commissioners. þÿ

of volunteers, to be used in case of necessity. The Commissioners have also left Stockton with an escort of some hundred U. S. troops, and it is confidently believed that if no obstacles are thrown in their way by revengeful or interested men, they will be able to form treaties with the mountain tribes and thus give quiet to the country. They are men of the right stamp, acquainted with the Indian character, and disposed to deal justly with them, we believe. The weather has continued dry, and, for winter, wonderfully warm ; sometimes as high as 75 degrees and seldom as low as 50 ; last evening it was at 47. We have not had five inches of rain since last March. The fear now is that we shall have no more rain ; the consequences of which will be severe disappointment to those engaged in the dry diggings and perhaps fatal to the stock and agricultural interests. Our Legislature has been battling for many things, but has won few victories. The fundamental colors in painting,

those by means of which all tints possible are obtained, are White, Black, Ye! loyv, Red, and Blue, and tor grcatei facility Green is added; Gray is a mixture of black and white ; Green a mix ture of yelloyv and blue ; Violet and Indigo are mixtures of red and blue, eh etc. The most important of the primitive colors, that which it is the most essential to render perfectly innocuous and unchangeable, is White, which enters into the composition of nearly all paint- The White exclusively employed now is the white oxyd or carbonate of lead, of which that called the white of silvei is only a more perfect variety. This brief enumeration shows us that the great and difficult problem presented, which Mr. I.eclaire sought to find a solution of, with so resolute a purpose, may he summed up in the production of, First. þÿ A Wh'te, dazzling, unchangeable, inoffensive, and endowed at the same time with all the desirable properties of white lead. For several years Mr. Leclnire has made exclusive and successful use of Ins various discoveries in colors and the drying oil. The experience of every day, made cn the largest scale in more ban six thousand public and private establishments þÿ the Departments of War and Public Works, the Bank of France, the Prefecture of Police, the Railroad Depots, etc., demonstrate, or rather establish beyond question, the following facts : þÿ First. þÿ The new colors with their
base of zinc, manganese, etc., are not injurious to the health of the workmen employed in their manufacture, the painters who use them, or the occupants of freshly painted houses. In the es-

<D 2$ b 'I a A '? 3 tablishment of Mr. Leclaire an average of a dozen workmen were formerly attacked with þÿpainter c s olic yearly, and some, more unfortunate, suffered five or six attacks of this dreadful disease. þÿ Since the introduction of the oxyd of zinc, and the oil prepared with manganese, not a single workman has been poisoned. Second. þÿ The new colors are infinitely more solid and durable than the old; they are not affected by sulphurous vapors ! they preserve, everywhere and always, their primitive tints, even in sulphuric bath-rooms ; and they have a property still more precious, namely when they are cleaned by simple washing they resume their original brightness; while the old colors, when washed even with acids, which dissolves a portion, remain dull and spotted, and for the simple reason that everything which decomposes stains them. I have had the opportunity of conversing with him on the subject, and could not conceal my astonishment at the import of his mission. In an advertisement, which appeared in your paper of the 27th Feb. last, all those persons, who hare the welfare of the colony at heart were invited to attend a meeting on the 10th day of the follow ing month. When the day arrived, every hotly was anxious to know the purport of the meeting; particularly as there were various idle rumours alloat, concerning the object of it. These idle reports, however, died away, as soon as the result of the meeting was known, whose real object was said to he, to petition Ilis Majesty again for compensation to former owners of non-predial slaves. The people were elated at the idea of trying once more to obtain this desirable God-send ; and were happy to see that a committee was formed, to take the necessary steps for carrying these measures into execution. It was also resolved, to lay the petition before the public, at a subsequent meeting, which would he convened for that purpose. Since this Ma þÿreh mn ting the inhabitants have been anxiously looking for the appointed day, which was to throw some further light on the subject ; hut up to this moment nothing is publicly known, either as to its beginning or its end þÿ a dead silence is strictly observed by the members of the committee. These gentlemen have been reminded in two subsequent communications, inserted in the St. Croix Avis, of the task, w hich they undertook to perform; yet they maintain the same silence, and, as it were, have

buried the matter in oblivion. There is not a word to he heard of the petition þÿ no reason assigned why it is not ready þÿ and nothing at all said, to satisfy 1 lie people, as to the long delay, which this all-important subject has met with. Shall I pronounce it as humbug? Or is it the mountain in labor once more ? We will see. In the meantime any information on this subject, will he gladh received. Let us, therefore, hope soon to hear that " the members of the committee" are lip and doing. I am, Sir, Tour obedient servant, ' Christiansted, 10th May 1851. O. 1\

IN, in command of the "Erebus" and " Terror," having on board one hundred and thirtyeight souls, set sail from England on the 19th ot May, 184.», in search of a north west passage. On the £<Jlh of July, sixty-eight days afterward, tlny were seen by a passing whaler moot id to an iceberg near the centre of Baffin's Bay; since which time no intelligence oi their fate has been received. No special anxiety w as entertained respecting them until t lie beginning of 18 1-' for the commander had intimated th t the voyage would probably continue fir three years, and that they might lie the first to announce their own return, lint as month a Iter month passed away without bringing any tidings, an anxious and painful sympathy sprung up in the public mind, and the British Government determined that searches for the missing vessels should he made in three different quarters by three separate ex peditions fitted out for that purpose. Oge quarter, however, that region known as Boothia, where there was a probability ot success, was beyond the scope of these expeditions, and Lade Franklin determined In organize an expedition to explore tiiat region. For ibis purpose she appropriated ail the means under her control; and a subscription was opened to supply the deficiency. The "Prince Albert," a ketch ol less than ninety Ions burden, measuring in length about seventy-two feet, and seventeen in breadth, w as-purchased

for ihe expedition. She was taken to Aberdeen to he fitted up; a double planking wu- put upon Iter, by way of pea-jacket to lit her for lur arctic vn\age, and a crew of fourteen canny , Scotchmen, secured by the promise of double pay. Captain Forsyth, of the Royal Navy, proffered his gratuitous services as commander. Attached to the expedition, having special charge of | the stores and scientific instrument:, j with the express understanding that he should head one of the ex; hiring parties to lie sent out from Regent's Inlet, was Mr. W. Par km Snow, from whose Journal we propose to draw up some | account ot' the pleasures of sailing through the ice. Mr. Snow seems to have been precise ly t lie man for such an undertaking. He j left America at three days' notice to j join any expedition which might lie sent out by Lady Franklin. With an artivc. i hopeful temperament, never so happy as in a gale of wind, if it was only blow- I ing the right way, he rushed to ihe cm- | brace of the Arctic Snow s with as much alacrity as though they were kinsmen as well as namesakes. He had, moreover, a happy faculty of turning his hand to every tiling, and no disposition to hide his talent in a napkin. A physician had been engaged for the vessel; hut when, two days before sailing, the (lis | ciplc of Esculapius saw the diminutive craft, he declined to proceed: þÿ Mr. Snow volunteered to perform his duties; lie

had read a little medicine at odd hours; and hy the aid of itees's Guide, and Sniec's Broadsheet, his practice was uniformly successful þÿ either in spite of, or 011 account of, his informal professional training. The sailors, as might he expected from their Scotch blood, were desirous of having religious worship on hoard: þÿ Mr. Snow offered his services as chaplain, reading and expounding the Scriptures, and olYcriug up prayer. On the 6th of June, 1H.50, the Prince Albert set sail from Aberdeen ; a fortnight brought them within two hundred miles of the shores of G i eenland. Then came, for a week, a succession of hea\y gales, which drove them back upon their course; so that in six days their progress was not more than a dozen miles. Tiie 1st of July, however found tlieni oil' Gape Pareweii. Sonic idea of the multifarious occupations of the inany-ofliceil Mr. Snow, at a time when his proper duties had not commenced, may be gathered t'roin his description of I.IKE ON sill I'ilo Alio. \t half-past six i used to turn out ; and, warm or cold, wet or dry, take an imine bate ablution in the pure and natural element. For half an hour I would t hen walk on deck, fair or foul; and, a little before eight, examine the men's forecastle; see to their condition, and whether any of them were sick; and if so, give them medicine. At eight hells, I would then take the chronometrical time for Captain Forsyth, while he observed the altitude of the sun, to get our longitude. Latterly 1 used, hy his

desire, to take a set of sights also myself, taking the tune from a common watch, and comparing it afterward with tiii! chronometer. Chronometers were then wound up by nie, and the thermometer, barometer, Ac., registered. At eight o'clock the two mates went to breakfast ; the captain and I getting ours soon after them. During the forenoon, I had to attend to the stores, provisions, Ac.; write inv accounts, journals, and other papers; and at noon worked up the ship's reckoning, the observations, and wrote the ship's log, ex 'mining our present position and future course. The mates had their dinner at noon : the captain and 1 at three p. it.; after which, a stroll for an hour or so on deck was taken hy both of us. Ten came round at six, and at eight p. M. I used to try the temperature of the air on deck, and of the sea. Alter that, we would read together in the stern cabin. At ten, we would take our hot grog; and, generally about eleven, when free from rough weather or the neighborhood of ice, turn in for the night. þÿ Very little candle was required below at night, as there was seldom more than an hour or two's darkness during any part of our voyage, until we were returning. It was not long after this date, moreover, that we had continued daylight through the whole twenty-four hours." The principal obstruction and danger in arctic navigation arises from the ice ;
