From these crystal plains rise sometimes isolated, sometimes in groups, elevations of thirty or more feet in height, called hummocks. Dr. Scoresby once saw a field so free from hummocks and fissures that a coach might have traversed it for leagues in a straight direction, without obstruction. In May or June these fields begin to drift along in solemn procession to the south west ward, in which direction, they hold their steady course, whether made to in calm or in spite of adverse winds. þÿ \V hen these floating continents emerge from the drift ice which had hitherto protected them, they are shattered and broken up by the long, deep swell of tlie ocean. A ground-swell, hardly perceptible in the open sea, will break up a field in a few hours. These fields sometimes acquire a rotary motion, which gives their circumference a velocity of several miles an hour producing a tremendous shock when one impinges upon another. " A body of more than ten thousand millions of tons in weight,' says Dr. Scorcsby, "meeting with resistance when in motion, produces consequences scarcely possible to conceive. 1 ne strongest ship is hut an insignificant impediment between two fields in motion. Great excitement prevailed at San I ranciseo, when fhe steamer left, owing to a scries of disgraceful robberies and murders there. The Pacific News savs : The more immediate cause of the existing excitement, was the recent attempt to kill, and the robbery of Mr. Janson, and the shooting of the Frenchman at the Adclphi Theatre, on Monday evening last ; both outrages of the most deliberate and murderous character, and both alike without any mitigating circumstances. Saturday afternoon, an examination was held before Justice Shepherd, of the two Australian men. Stuart and Wililrcd, in the Recorder's court-room, on the charge of assaulting and robbing Mr. Janson, the room and balcony being crowded by spectators. At the close ol the examination something was said about admitting them to bail, when the crowd, incensed at such a prospect, made a rush for the prisoners, breaking down benches, desks, railing and everything which impeded their progress, driving the police officers before them. Fortunately for the culprits, the Washington Guards, who had been parading in honor of the day, happened to lie near at hand, and being called on by the authorities, drove back the crowd, and cleared the court-room at the point of the bayonet. Rut for this, both of the accused would have been stringing between heaven and earth, within the next fifteen minutes, at the end of'strong hempen cord, already prepared lor the occasion, and in the hands of determined men.

\\ bile the guard were driving back the crowd, the prisoners were taken out the back way, and let down liaougli a trap door into the station house below. A meeting of citizens was held on I lie evening of the 4th, the call for which demanded the most vigorous measures of Lynch Law against the " Anarchists." " The laws," says the call, offer lis no protection. " Let every man be his own executioner !" The meeting passed off quietly, but amidst great excitement. Motions were proceed to the jail and execute the prisoners at once. These, however, were voted down.. The design was to select a jury, give the prisoners a popular trial, with the intention of carrying the verdict rendered and sentence imposed into instant effect. The jury disagreed, however, and the people, becoming worn out with the excitement, dispersed without attempting the rescue of the accused from the officers of justice. Another murder had been committed on the 20th February in the mountains, near Murphy's Diggings. An Englishman named Richard or Joseph llalfliead had gone from the French Camp to Mokelumne Hill, prospecting, and had selected a claim. On returning for bis tools and camp utensils, it is supposed the spot where lie was found dead, on the 20th, and was shot while sitting or laying down, lie was discovered by a party of miners, and bis body taken by his friends and buried. þÿ lie was formerly from Rcdford, near London, where his friends reside. Robbery was undoubtedly the object of the murder, but the perpetrators did

not probably get five dollars as their reward. Another fire had occurred at San Fran cisco. It originated in an unoccupied building on itryant Place, corner of Rush, and immediately communicated with the store of Mr. Randall, corner of Rush and Sansonie streets, destroying in its course the Museum Hotel, Shamrock House, and New Bedford þÿHotel. The late Hans Christian Orsted, < ; rand Cross of the order of Dannebrog, Privy Councellor of the first class, which confers the title of Excellency, Professor of Natural Philosophy, and from 1815 Secretary to the lloyal Society ot Copenhagen, was born, August 14, 1777, in the little town of Rudkjdping, on the Danish island of Langcland, where his father was an apothecary, and known as a man of a singularly well-stored mind. His younger brother was for a long time Prime Minister to the Ring of Denmark, and was renowned for his legal erudition. The poor circumstances of the parents, and the absence of educational establishments at ltudkjuping, made it difficult to have t he boys educated. þÿ From a Herman in the neighbourhood tliev learnt Herman ; the eldest then taught himself arithmetic from an old school-book, and having advanced so far, taught the new-gained knowledge to his brother, llotli were eager learners, and inspired and aided each other. Their Herman master taught them also a little Latin, but they had not much lime to spare for the acquisition of learning alone, they must help to earn the. daily means of living; and Hans Christian, in his twelfth year, was obliged to assist his father. 1 lie occupation was not, however, one of dull drudgery to him ; his quickly observing and clearly reasoning mind was soon fixed with pleasure upon the study of chemistry, which became his lavourife subject, but not to the neglect of more general science, history, and literature.

In the November of 1800 Orsted was faculty of medicine of the Danish Di- appointed assistant in chemistry to I the versity of Copenhagen, at which he had already passed the usual course. S'o earlv as 1804, he published, in Herman. researches into the identity ot electrical and chemical forces. In 1807 the idea occurred to him that electricity and magnetism bad some nihility, and he " proposed to try, whether electricity the most latent had any action on the magnet." The idea was not lost sight of; but, for the next tw elve years, no experiment was made to establish it as a tact. Orsted was busily engaged, during that period, writing, travelling, lecturing and establishing a system ol chemistry, so that it was not until the winter of jslO that he was enabled, by positive experiment, to convince the world that his long-followed theory was a scientific truth. The Professor's own account of of the first series of the Annals of his discovery is published in vol. xxi., " Philosophy," and the results of the determining experiments arc given in the second volume of the new series, 1821, m a paper entitled " Historic Sketch of Electro- Magnetism," published at the time anonymously, but since known to be from the pen of Faraday. In 1820 Orsted made known the fact referred to above, that "a magnetised needle placed near a wire connecting the poles of

3 To <0 a I X A T I So a galvanic pile was forced to change its direction ; and always, when the current was sufficiently strong, that the needle took a position at right angles to the wire : that, if the wire were sunk on either side (lie needle, so as to conic into the horizontal plane in which the needle was allowed to move, there was no motion of the needle in that plane, but that it manifestly attempted to move in a vertical circle ; and that, whenever the direction of the current along the wire was reversed, the needle made half a revolution, and reversed the direction of its poles so as still to keep at right angles to the wire. Orsted showed that these results proved that the movements of the needle were in a circle round the wire." It was twenty years since Volta had constructed his pile. In the interim it had occurred to others as well as Orsted that there existed some relationship between the mysterious forces of galvanism and magnetism, but every effort to prove the fact had failed. Orsted, from the first moment he caught the thought, never doubted, that he should be able to work out the secret. The needle turning from its polos and seeking to revolve round the connecting wire ol flie battery, was to liiiu the triumph of flic cherished thought of years. Everywhere throughout Europe, the greatest chemists took eager hold of the discovery. Arago, Riot, Savart, Savary, Davy, Camming, Faraday, Berzelius, De la Rive, Sweiger, Nobili, Scebeck, and þÿ most successful of all þÿ Ampere, set on

foot researches founded upon the discovery. Orsted, the poor apothecary's son þÿ who had taught himself, and from very boyhood had worked for his living as lie learned þÿ obtained a world-wide fame, and lived to see, in the establishment of the Electric Telegraph, the

if we may use the phrase, he had hunted down. On the Ifitli of November, 1821), the Council of' the Royal Soeiciy awarded him the Copleyan Medal for his electromagnetic discoveries ; and in the same year lie received the Hold Medal ot' the French Academy. In 1821 lie was still further honoured by being elected a foreign member of the Royal Society þÿ conferring with the medal a distinction justly appreciated abroad as the highest which England can confer upon scientific merit. But orsted also engaged in experiments of an entirely different character. In 1822 lie contrived a very ingenious instrument for measuring the compression of water. In 182(1, he instituted a set of experiments on the compression of gases, which resulted in establishing, under the highest degrees of pressure, Mariotti's law þÿ hitherto proved only under small degrees of pressure þÿ " that all kinds of gases, under all degrees of pressure in which they retain their aeriform state, are uniformly compressible." In 1842, on tbe death of the celebrated botanist, De Candolle, of Geneva, Orsted was elected one of the eight foreign members of the French Academy of

Sciences having been previously, for several years, a corresponding member ih the Physical Class. There were last year, but five of the foreign members of the Royal Society of London, who could boast of holding a place amongst the honoured eight in the French Academy. Orsted again visited England in 184»», and was present at the meeting of the British Association at Southampton, þÿ On that occasion he was spoken of, in connexion with his great discovery, as one whose name could never be forgotten in the history of physical science. Last year, as the fiftieth anniversary of Orsted's academic life approached, bis fellow-citizens resolved to distinguish the occasion, and the King, sharing the enthusiasm, determined to bestow upon his world-honoured subject an especial mark of his Royal favour. On the 7lii of November Orsted was wailed upon by deputations of" the beads of faculties, students oftlie Diversity, pupils of the '. Polytechnic Institution, the Association of Industry, and a large number of personal friends and gentlemen of high rank. Dr. J. N. Madwig, Minister of Public. Instruction, presented him, in the name of His Majesty, with a life residence in the Roval Hardens of Fredericksberg, recently the residence of the Danish poet Ohlerisclilager, and, at the same time, the distinction .of the highest civil rank in the State was given to liim. marble were given by the citizens, one for his family, the other to be placed in the Polytechnic School. In 1850 Orsted published, at Copenhagen, a work entitled " The Spirit in Nature; being a popular Contribution towards Illustrating the Spiritual Influpractical usefulness of the idea which, ences of Nature ;" and in 1851 a second edition of the first part was published. " Orsted, " writes a friend of his from Copenhagen, " was loved and esteemed by every one who knew him. Men of the highest rank were happy to associate with him, ami held it an honour to be admitted to his family circle, lie was learned, of the highest morality and honour, and the best spouse A father." Orsted did not long live to enjoy his beautiful residence ; after a short illness, lie died, surrounded by a numerous family, on the morning of the ftth of March, at the age of seventy-four, at the residence so recently conferred on him hv his Sovereign. taking the first ice. "We had come so quickly and unexpectedly upon this "stream" (not having seen it, owing to the thick weather, until close aboard of it), that promptitude of decision and movement was absolutely necessary. It was one of those moments when the seaman conies forward, and by boldly acting, either in (lie one way or the other shows what lie is made of. In the present ease the question instantly arose as to whether the vessel should at once run through tli e ice now before her, or wait until clearer and milder weather came. Tite mate, as ice-master, was asked by the captain which, in his opinion, was best, lie advised heaving to, to windward of it, and waiting. The second mate was then asked ; and lie, without knowing the other's opinion, strongly urged the ne cessitv of running through at once. Captain Forsyth, using his own judgment, very wisely decided upon the latter, and accordingly run t lie ship on. \nd a pretty sight, too, it was, as the " Prince Albert" under easy and working sail, in a moment or two more entered the intricate channels that were presented to her between numerous bergs and pieces oi ice, rough and smooth, large and small, new and old, dark and white. It, was hazy weather, snowing o and rainiiur r> at the time; and all hands basing been summoned on deck, were wrapped in their oil-skin dresses and waterproof overcoats. Standing on the topsailyard was the second mate conning the ship ; half-way up the weather rigging clung the captain, watching and direct-

ing as necessary ; while aft, on the rais ed counter near the wheel, stood the cliiet mate telling the helmsman how to steer. This being the first ice in an\ large and continuous quantity that we had met, I looked at it with some curiosity. The moment we had entered within the outer edge of the stream the water became as smooth as a common pond on shore; and it was positively a pretty sight to see that little vessel dodging in and out and threading her way among the numerous pieces of ice that beset her proper and direct course. The ice itself presented a most beautiful appearance both in color and form, being variegated in every direction. \\ e were soon in the very thick of it ; and before five minutes had elapsed from our first taking it we could see no apparent means ot either going on or retracting our steps. But it was well managed, and after about an hour's turning hither and thither, this way and that way, straight and crooked, we got fairly through, and found clear water beyond. " Throughout the night the wind blew a complete hurricane, and the short high sea was perfectly furious ; lashing about in all directions with the madness of a maelstrom, and with a

violence that, apparently, nothing could resist. Heavy squalls, with sharp sleet and snowstorms from the southward, added to the fearful tempest that was raging. It was impossible to see three miles ahead, the weather being so thick. Occasionally an iceberg would dart out through the mist, heaving its huge body up and down in frightful motion, now advancing, next receding, and again approaching with any thing but pleasant proximity. Our little vessel, however, as usual, stood it well. Could we have divested ourselves of the reality of the scene, it might have been likened to a fancy picture, in which some strange and curious dance was being represented between the sea, the ice, and the ship ; the latter, by the aid of the former, gallantly lifting herself to, and then declining from the other. But it was too real ; and the greater danger of the land being possibly near, was too strongly impressed upon our minds, to allow any visionary feeling possess us at the to time. It was the worst and most dangerous night we had yet had, and hardly a man on board rested until the height of it was past." Soon after this a boat's crew was sent ashore for water, where in a lonely spot they discovered the grave of an European, with an inscription on a rude wooden tablet at its head, stating that ! voice in ' John Huntley of Shetland, was buried j there in August, 1847." The sailors i replaced the board which had blown down; and left the solitary grave, with the humble tribute of a wish for the

repose of the poor fellow's soul. A few days later while on shore, .Mr. Snow i for was spectator of the OVERTURN OF AN ICEBF.RIi. " I was speedily awakened to reality 1 v a sudden noise like the cracking of j purposes of a family instrument. This some mighty editice of stone, or the j combination, we believe, is to be found bursting of several pieces of ordnance, lire the sound of that noise had vibrated on the air, a succession of reports like the continued discharge of a heavy tire of musketry, interspersed with the occasional roar of cannon, followed upon one another, for the space of perhaps two minutes; when, suddenly, my eye was arrested by the oscillation of a moderate-sized iceberg not far beneath my feet, in a line away from the hill I was upon ; and the next moment it tottered, and with a sidelong inclination, cut its way into the bosom of the sea upon which it had before been reclining. Hoar upon roar pealed in echoes from the mountain heights on every side : the wide sea-bird arose with fluttering wings and rapid flight as it proceeded to a quarter where its quiet would be less disturbed: the heretofore peaceful water presented the appearance of a troubled ocean after a fierce gale of wind ; and, amid the varied sounds now heard, human voices from the boat came rising up on high in honest English þÿ strangely striking on the þÿear hailing to know if I had seen the 'sun,' and also whether I wanted them to join me. peace at home. It is just as possible to keep a calm house as a clean house, a cheerful house, an orderly house as a furnished house, if the heads set themselves todo so. W here is the dilliculty of consulting each other's weakness, as well as each other's wants; each other's tempers, as well as each, other's health; each other's comfort, as well as each other's character V Oh ! it is by leaving the peace at home to chance, instead of pursuing it by system, that so many houses are unhappy. It deserves notice, also, that almost any one can he courteous and forbearing and patient in a neighbor's house. If anything go wrong, or be out of time, or disagreeable there, it is made the best of, not the worst; even efforts arc made to excuse it, and to show that it is not felt ; or, if

felt, it is attributed to accident, not design : and this is not only easy, but natural, in the house of a friend. I will not, therefore, believe that what is so natural in the house of another is impossible at home, but maintain, without fear, that all the courtesies of social life may be upheld in domestic societies. þÿ A husband, as willing to be pleased at home and as anxious to please as in his neighbor's house : and a wife, as intent on making things comfortable every day to her family, as on set days to her guests, could not li d to make their own home happv Let us not evade the point of three remarks by recurring to the maxim about allowances of temper. It is worse tiian folly to refer to our temper, unless we could prove that we ever gained anything good by giving way to it. Fits of ill humor punish us quite as much, if not more, than those thev are vented upon; and it actually requires mou effort, and inflicts more pain to give them up, 1 dan would be requisite to avoid them. þÿ Phillip.
